speakeroldname: Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: TABLING OF COPY OF OCCUPATIONAL COUNSELLING GUIDE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate requested an up to date copy of the occupational counselling guide prepared for the use of the immigration branch of my department. I have furnished him with a copy, and I should like to table the latest copy of this guide at this time. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate will recall that on an earlier occasion I tabled a copy of the guide in the house in response to a request made by him on June 25, 1958.
The occupational counselling guide is a monthly report compiled by immigration officers throughout Canada, providing factual information as to employment conditions in different parts of the country. As its name implies, it is used to advise prospective immigrants with various kinds of occupational skills and to assist them in deciding where to settle. The guide does not purport to list specific employment opportunities in the various localities but indicates simply that on the basis of the assessment made by experienced immigration officers in the areas concerned an immigrant with a particular occupation will be better able to settle in one locality than in another, and that even though there may not be an immediate opening in a given area for his specific occupation, the prospects there are generally good for his eventual settlement.
The occupational guide is compiled on a monthly basis and contains for each locality and each occupational classification one of three designations, the letter "G" indicating good prospects for establishment in a particular occupation in a particular area; the letter "L" indicating limited prospects for establishment of immigrants with a particular occupation in a particular area, and a blank space indicating little or no prospects.
I should perhaps add that while it is the immigration branch of my department which
is responsible for the preparation and compilation of the guide, the material which is supplied for this purpose by our field immigration officers is obtained from many sources, including employers. Information is also available from local offices of the national employment service. We are continuing our efforts by every appropriate means to coordinate the information supplied in this way to our officers overseas.

Mr. Chairman, while it may seem a sweeping statement, it is nevertheless true to say that never since confederation has it been possible for a postmaster general to record in one annual report, as I will today, such a wide range of new development and progress both internally and in service to the public.
Just a few of the more sweeping changes and developments of the past 12 months have been reorganization within the department and the creation of a comptroller's branch; new equipment developments in stamp vending machines, mail mobiles, delivery carts, plastic mail boxes; extension of service to the public through new letter carrier areas and rural mail routes; improvements in service to the public in fields such as parcel deliveries, the delivery of mail to apartment residents and an increase in accounting post offices; progress in our electronic sorting machine and other equipment; trials of a new mail flow system; new philatelic enterprises and an organized plan to promote interest in Canada in foreign countries by philatelic means; a project to make new stamps available as an aid in the teaching process in Canada; advances in our internal training techniques; improvement in staff relations through closer co-operation with employee associations; plans for a postal history museum; new regulations covering an important category of mail known as householder mail; statistical evidence of improvement in our service as demonstrated by a reduction in complaints received; and various other matters, some of which I will deal with in my report and others which I will not even have time to mention.

During the year we opened 28 revenue post offices to serve small rural communities, and 97 sub-post offices to give local service in urban centres. We also established two new staff post offices, two new postal stations and two new letter carrier depots. Finally, and reflecting a substantial improvement in the housing of our postal activities, we occupied 105 new federal buildings.
Proceeding with our program to streamline our internal organization, which last year saw the creation of our engineering and development branch, we have this year created a new comptroller's branch. This brings under the immediate direction of one senior official, a man of wide experience in accounting practices and postal problems, the internal accounting systems of the department, the operation and control over budgetary arrangements and our purchasing and stores operations. Improved control of these operations will result in a substantial increase in efficiency in these fields.
Canada has recently played a much more important part in the international postal sphere by reason of her position as vice president of the executive and liaison committee of the universal postal union, and in addition we have concentrated much attention on our postal relations with the United States. Currently we are studying revisions to a postal convention between our two countries, a revision which is long overdue.

Our country has proportionately an extremely large volume of international mail, and since much of this travels by air we have made many changes to improve this type of service. The advent of jet aircraft on international routes is beginning to make a tremendous impact on the speed with which mail travels. To cite but one example, by this fall it will be possible for mail to leave London, England at 3.05 p.m. local time and arrive in Vancouver, B.C., at 11.15 p.m. local time, using the regular T.C.A. services. This gives some idea of the possibilities we envision for mail handling and transport by air.
At home, widespread increases and improvements in service have been inaugurated. During the year, for instance, letter carrier delivery service was established for the first time in five communities; Alma, Quebec and Stoney Creek, Georgetown, Whitby and Elliot Lake, Ontario. A total of 29 new walks were established in these communities to serve some 13,523 calls.
In addition to these new services, 306 letter carrier walks were placed in operation during the year to permit the extension of service in other communities already enjoying letter carrier service. A total of some 154,604 new calls, including about 78,360 additional calls on established routes, were added in this way. Beyond these letter carrier services, some 8,353 families were afforded service through group mail boxes

pending the eventual provision of door to door mail delivery when postal requirements have been met.
To improve delivery service in rural areas we have inaugurated during the past year 89 new rural routes and have also made 1,006 extensions to such routes.
In order to improve service after regular post office hours we have expanded our program of installing, at strategic points across the country, government-owned postage stamp vending machines which give full face value in stamps for the money deposited. Five hundred new machines were placed in operation during the past year, bringing the total number owned by the department to 2,026.
In the same field we also have under development at the present time a stamp vending machine designed to meet somewhat less rugged conditions when it is installed inside post offices. Through the use of this machine we hope to avoid some of the pressure on our wicket sales and reduce the occasional line-ups which occur, thus ensuring even better service to the public. We are also developing a completely automatic model which will be actuated by the mere depositing of a coin, so the patron will not have to pull a plunger or exert any effort whatsoever. I guess this is the limit of automation, short of providing the public with the coins to put in the machines, and we have no plans for doing that at the moment.
To improve the postal services available in smaller communities in Canada we have considerably extended the number of accounting post offices because at these it is possible to buy money orders in larger denominations than at non-accounting offices. In 1957-58 we changed from non-accounting to accounting status 66 such offices; in 1958-59, 113 and in 1959-60, 169. Hon. members can see the tremendous increase in this field of activity.
Last year at this time I announced that the department had undertaken an experiment with a three-wheeled vehicle called a mail-mobile for door to door mail delivery service in suburban areas. The original experiment was undertaken in British Columbia with a United States machine, and proved so successful that the original five machines have been augmented by a further 50 vehicles, including 15 which have been developed by a Canadian manufacturer. These are now undergoing extensive testing in other parts of the country.
We are now about to try yet another mobile piece of equipment; letter carrier delivery carts, to which I referred yesterday in answer
Supply-Post Office
to a question in the house. The best comparison I can offer for these are the twowheeled carts which one sees so often on golf courses to carry the golf bag of players. There is some considerable doubt that these are going to work out, and we can foresee a number of problems in their use. None the less, they deserve a trial in accord with our present policy-and I think I can almost say our new policy under this administration-of constantly testing new ideas and equipment which appear to have merit.
Among the most commented on pieces of equipment we have introduced this year are the new plastic letter boxes being installed, one or two to a city, in most of the major centres across Canada. Their design is most attractive and has been widely commended by a number of people, including even Mr. Alan Jarvis in a press article on the subject. The plastic material, with the colour impregnated, requires little of the upkeep or repainting which is now a costly factor in connection with existing metal boxes. While it is still too early to completely assess their potential, the probability is they will be most successful, and if this is the case we will introduce them widely across Canada as the older boxes are retired.
We have made many improvements during the past year in our service to the public. For example, we have developed a new procedure for the handling of parcels which we are unable to deliver because the patron is not at home when we make the first call. Previously these had been returned to the local post office, and the only course of action open to the patron was to call for them. While this course of action is still open to patrons, they have the option now of having the item delivered a second time at a prearranged time for a fee of 25 cents. Our trial of this service has been so enthusiastically received that we will soon establish the system on a regular basis throughout Canada.
Another of the several adjustments we have made to improve service to the public concerns the delivery to individual residents of apartment buildings of mail matter requiring direct personal contract. In the past, in many such cases the letter carrier was only permitted to leave a card in the mail box notifying the patron that such items could be picked up at the post office. Now these items, including such things as registered mail, short paid articles, C.O.D. packages and items too large to fit in apartment mail boxes, are delivered by the letter carrier to individual residents of apartment buildings in the same manner as for individual houses.
One way in which we control the quality of our service is through a very careful

analysis of all the complaints we receive. It is a measure of our constant improvement that despite a steady increase in mail volume -and hon. members will recall that I said it had increased by 100 million pieces this year-the number of inquiries or complaints dropped by more than 10,000 in each of the past two years, so that while in 1957-58 we had 112 inquiries or complaints for every million pieces handled, this dropped to 106 in 1958-59 and to 101 in the past year.
We are still trying to improve, but it is getting harder when one realizes that we have already reached the point where only one one hundredth of one per cent of mail handled resulted in an inquiry or complaint, and that in many of these cases investigation revealed the complaint to be unfounded.
I am sure that some ox my friends in this house will wish to ask me about robberies of post office vehicles and buildings, and to inquire as to what steps are being taken to safeguard the mails from depredations of this type. I would like to state that during the last two years or more we have built up a greatly increased security-mindedness on the part of postal employees at all levels. With the assistance of the Department of Public Works we have improved the security of our buildings and added to our protective equipment.
For comparative and statistical purposes within the department we list as losses by burglary the items on which we can place an accurate or approximately accurate monetary value, including cash, stamps, denominative money orders, and so on. The results of our efforts to reduce the loss attributable to burglaries are illustrated by the fact that we have reduced the net average loss per burglary from $1,262 in 1958-59 to $983 in the last fiscal year, and the total figure has dropped from $448,248 to $385,663.
However, it is important to realize that these loss figures for statistical purposes are actually greatly in excess of the loss to either the post office or the public treasury, because only the cash stolen is a complete loss. In many cases the postage stamps stolen cannot be disposed of by the thieves and are destroyed. In the case of money orders stolen, the picture is clear because they can be identified when they pass through the post office. In the last fiscal year, for example, denominative money orders having a potential value of $139,305 were stolen and included in the loss figures; on the other hand, the thieves succeeded in cashing only 20 of these at post offices and the total value thereof was only $201. In other words, a reported loss of $139,000 was in fact only a loss of $200.

More stringent regulations regarding the retention of cash in post offices have made possible the reduction of actual cash losses from an average of $84 per burglary in 195859 to an average of $70 in the last fiscal year.
Special attention has also been given to our methods of handling the dispatch of mail to ensure its protection in transit. In recent years, as you are aware, the railways have eliminated many of their trains and the post office has been forced more and more to resort to highway transport to deliver the mails swiftly and efficiently. Obviously the security problems of handling mail by truck are more complex than in hauling it by train. We have, however, recently developed new security measures for this purpose in co-operation with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the provincial police forces and the police staffs of the municipalities concerned. Unfortunately, to give details of these would merely provide information eagerly sought by prospective robbers and burglars, and I hope the committee and particularly the hon. member for St. Denis will not press me for such information. We cannot avoid every possibility of theft or of robbery on the highway, but in comparison with the general picture in this field throughout Canada our record is a favourable one, and reflects the results of the substantial efforts we are making.
Last year at this time I discussed developments in the electronic-mechanical mail sorta-tion system presently being developed by the Canada post office and destined for operational testing in the Montreal post office later this year. This is now undergoing the final stages of modification at the plant of Canadair Limited.
While we have great hopes and expectations for this particular equipment, which has been under development by the Canadian post office for a number of years, we can have no certainty as to the results until it has undergone extensive trials in actual postal operation. I feel, however, that the advances we have made in this direction during the past 15 months, since placing the development contract with Canadair, have been substantially greater than would have been the case had we attempted to undertake this stage of the work within the Post Office Department itself as was contemplated by the previous administration.
To operate the machine during its test period we are going to need a staff of specially trained people, and we are now well advanced on the training of supervisors and operators in this field. Also under construction for us at the present time in the United Kingdom is a unit of equipment designed to

mechanize the first operations performed on mail when it reaches a post office. These include the separation of letters and parcels, the facing up so the addresses are all in the same relative position and the stamps in the same place, the cancelling of the stamps and the initial division of the mail into that for local delivery and that to be forwarded to other points. The new equipment will be installed in the Winnipeg post office, probably in the first half of 1961, for evaluation under Canadian conditions, and it will represent a major step forward in the modernization of our operations, since previously the only one of the several operations it undertakes which was done by machinery was the actual cancellation of the stamps themselves.
We are also testing in Toronto at the present time a new mail-flow system by which, when the time arrives for mail which has been sorted to be removed from the sorting cases and dispatched, an announcement is made over a loudspeaker system and the sorter merely removes the mail and puts it on a moving belt underneath his table. Previously a considerable amount of pedestrian traffic was required since the mail was picked up individually from each case.
Our studies are continuing on possible methods of applying electronic data processing to the issue of postal money orders at post office wickets, and to the audit of these money orders at headquarters. Since we handle over 50 million money orders a year this is a field of considerable interest to us.
I must emphasize again, as I do each year when discussing these developments, that the programs on which we are working are not designed, and will not be allowed, to throw existing full-time postal employees out of work. However, they will bring about more efficient handling of our ever increasing mail volume without corresponding increases in staff.
About two years ago, after studying the whole question of improving post office operation through mechanization, I told the house that I felt it would take about five years to develop, install and test under operating conditions the necessary equipment and another five years following that to extend its operation generally throughout the postal service to all points where it could be effectively used. I see no reason to depart from this timetable which takes into account, on the one hand, the need for these measures and, on the other, the necessity that they be introduced at a rate which will enable the department to adjust to the changes without dislocation of staff or hardship to anyone.
During the past year probably no aspect of the postal service received more widespread publicity than our householder mail
Supply-Post Office
service, the system under which an advertiser may mail printed matter to all the householders in a given area without being required to have it individually addressed or stamped. The operation of this system has posed an increasing problem for some time, and the department has received many requests from various sources to make adjustments in it. Not the least of these pressures was from within the postal service itself, where both high-ranking officers and letter carriers complained that the mass of unaddressed mail matter was causing difficulties in maintaining a proper mail service. Another source of complaint on this subject was mail patrons themselves, many of whom resent such unsolicited matter in their mail.
As a result of these and other approaches the department carried out a full study of the problem from all possible angles. The resulting changes, first announced a few weeks ago, go into effect June 1. They will restrict the size of householder mail items, forbid irregular shapes and penalize heavy, bulky items. Generally speaking the new regulations have met with widespread approval, while at the same time Canada's advertising associations have accepted them without criticism or complaint.
During the year the post office produced five commemorative stamps. The subjects covered were the NATO anniversary, the Associated Country Women of the World, the royal visit, the St. Lawrence seaway and the plains of Abraham. In connection with the last, I should like to note that this stamp was recently named, by a well known philatelic journal published in the United Kingdom, as the best commonwealth stamp of the year, and one of the ten best stamps of the year produced by any nation.
Another very popular innovation of the past year has been the introduction of special cards, each bearing a number of our commemorative postage stamps to a total value of 50 cents, with a short outline of the reason for the stamp and the importance of the subject to Canada on the back of the card. These have been phenomenally attractive to tourists.
I have frequently expressed the view that commemorative stamps are, in effect, small billboards of Canada. To make sure that these billboards receive the widest possible distribution and attention, we have recently adopted the practice of sending first day covers of new commemorative stamps to prominent people and newspaper editors in many lands. I believe the number is between 50 and 60. We enclose a brief explanation of the event the stamp commemorates and other information about the background of

the particular issue. We have also adopted the practice of distributing information folders on each new stamp to teachers responsible for selected age groups in Canada's public schools. This we are doing through the active co-operation of all ten provincial departments of education, and first results indicate that the program has been both effective and appreciated.
We are also going to have in our new postal headquarters building, when it is opened next year, a postal history museum, and planning is now under way for this purpose. This will enable us to take out from our vaults and display to the public a great deal of material of interest to stamp collectors as well as exhibits and displays of material and equipment of wide general interest.
Another area in which we are attempting to streamline operations is in our office services. Here we have engaged in an extensive program of personnel training, and have introduced a uniform file control procedure throughout the department. Considerable savings also accrued to the department through the application of the incentive pay plan for typists and stenographers. Until recently, while the Post Office Department engaged in a very extensive program of training courses for its personnel, each course was directly related in a detailed way to some phase of postal activity. Such courses are very necessary and very valuable, but they have one shortcoming; while they increase technical proficiency they do comparatively little to develop the broad managerial skill of those participating.
As we progress in our development of post office operations there is a constantly increasing number of positions opening in our service where these same management skills are required, areas where new problems are concerned involving an intermixture of personnel relations, operating techniques and service to the public. To meet this challenge I asked that a management development course for some of our fairly senior personnel be undertaken and the first two groups, one in Ottawa and the other in Calgary, recently completed their work. At the moment it is impossible to pin down statistically the results of such training efforts, but there is every indication that the courses are of substantial benefit and are broadening and increasing the management ability of those who participate.
In any organization as large as the Post Office Department the relations between management and staff are of critical importance. We do not expect the employee

associations to see eye to eye with management on every matter, but I believe firmly that the more extended the discussions between the two groups, the more understanding and harmony there will be.
When I became Postmaster General such interchange of ideas was at a minimum. Today this has been substantially changed and there are regular full, free and frank discussions between management and the representatives of our staff associations on a wide variety of problems. We are not surrendering our right to make final decisions, and I have no intention of doing so; but now, unlike the past, before major decisions are made the views and observations of postal workers are taken into consideration, and this is a great help in arriving at the most satisfactory course for everybody concerned.
As a result of this and other changes I feel that staff relations within the department have improved substantially over the past three years, and one measure of this fact is the rate of turnover. Separations from the postal service continue at a level substantially below that of the civil service as a whole, and the rate for this year, in all categories, was 8 per cent.
During my term as Postmaster General I have had ample opportunity to study these men and women at their work. I have made a practice of dropping in unexpectedly and at odd hours of the day and night. I have been in offices at midnight; I have been in offices at 6 a.m., and I have been in offices at just about every interval between those two times. I never failed to be impressed with the employees' cheerfulness, their capability and their determination to do their work swiftly and well. I have found in the postal service a quality of devotion and integrity that is, perhaps, unusual in this day of materialism and mass production.
From the point of view of management, our changes and improvements in the past year add up to the most sweeping adjustment and development the Post Office Department has undergone since confederation. I have reviewed the reports of postmasters general for a number of years before 1957; none bristles as does the one I have just given with example after example of change, of adjustment, of improvement and of progress and, none the less, I have dealt with only some of our activities over the past year.
But mechanical equipment and advanced policies are not now, nor ever will be, the key to the operation of an efficient and successful postal service. The key to success is people, the 50,000 people who work at headquarters and in Canada's 11,500 post

offices; who drive courier trucks, walk letter carrier routes, ride our mail cars, operate our clerical services and, in more senior posts, direct postal activities generally. These are the men and the women who make Canada's postal service second to none in a field where service is a tradition and where that same tradition is very much alive.

Consequently, I think that the Postmaster General might at least have told us why he is unable to balance his department's budget, whereas in 1957, though we did not have the same returns, we nevertheless found a way to get a $5 million and even $10 million surplus. I wonder what would happen if all government departments wound up with deficits. I do not think he was of any help to the Minister of Finance in budgeting for $13 million surplus. Now that is quite different from what happened in the past and I do not think that the minister is responsible for the progress or improvements he referred to. I think these were routine activity, the result of departmental decisions and if new services have been inaugurated in rural mail delivery and mail carrier work, it was due to increased population or points of call in those areas. Therefore, I believe that, instead of telling us about the achievements of his staff the minister might have recalled the promises he made when sitting in the opposition and which have not been fulfilled after he became Postmaster General.
Mr. Chairman, just to refresh the Postmaster General's memory, let me remind him of what he had to say in 1954, when he was sitting on this side of the house. I quote from page 1119 of Hansard for January 14, 1954:
Summarizing what I have tried to set before the house today, may I say that, first, the government has used the post office to pile up huge surpluses in the past 20 years in direct contradiction of the policy of the Post Office Department in previous years.
I just wonder, Mr. Chairman, where the Postmaster General got that phrase "policy of the Post Office Department in previous years", according to which policy we have to have deficits. It is just beyond me, Mr. Chairman.
The minister went on to say:
-second, the government, for reasons best known to itself, has forced the post office to subsidize the operation of Trans-Canada Air Lines in order that Trans-Canada Air Lines might show a profit:
Mr. Chairman, if you look at the Postmaster General's report, you find that T.C.A. is making more money today than at the time the Postmaster General, sitting in the opposition, denounced the payments made to T.C.A., suggested that those contracts were made secretly and that no information was available about them. What particulars are we getting today from the Postmaster General? None.
The present Postmaster General also made this statement:

Third, the government, through excessive use of the franking privilege by its various departments, is burdening the post office with costs of other departments.
Mr. Chairman, I ask the Postmaster General whether he has changed that method of administration. He has been heading the department for three years. Has he made the change he was advocating when he used to sit in the opposition? I doubt it. Not only do I doubt it, but the minister said in 1957 that the then postmaster general was misrepresenting the revenue and expenditures of his department because the lands, buildings and equipment which were supplied by the Department of Public Works should have been included in the statement of profits and loss of the Post Office Department.
Has the Postmaster General changed this accounting system? I do not think he has. He even went further at that time when he said:
Fourth, users of first class mail are thus forced to pay more than their share of their services in order to subsidize losses suffered on other classes of mail which are quite legitimate, but which should be properly charged to the general revenue of government.
I think he was comparing first class mail with third class mail. Is the loss resulting from third class mail now entered under general government expenditures? I do not think so, Mr. Chairman. Therefore, what the Postmaster General then considered black he now finds white.
We also remember that he was opposed to higher postage rates. Have postage rates changed since the Postmaster General has been heading the Post Office Department? I do not think so. Indeed he now seems opposed to anything that could yield profits. As I said a moment ago, his department shows an increase in revenue of $16 million, and the minister tells us: "We only have a small deficit of $173,000". If, at least, the situation of the civil servants in his department had been improved.
We heard him a moment ago tell us about the good relations between himself and his officials. Now I have proof to the contrary. He stated that they are more and more satisfied with their positions. If the minister entertains that idea, I shall tell him that he has been at the head of the department for the past three years, but when the general election comes around, postal employees will know better days.
The minister spoke about the civil service commission. You wonder whether

people are pleased? It is a well-known fact that, throughout the country, civil servants, letter carriers, postal employees, are dissatisfied with the little concern shown for their claims and requests.
Having said that, I want to quote a statement from the 1957 Hansard, pages 1983-4, when hon. members of this government were on the opposition benches:
Has the minister ever made any recommendation to the civil service commission to point out the situation and the outcome which I think he will agree is peculiar to his department? Has he ever made any attempt to have the situation straightened out?
There is also that other statement, on page 2744 of Hansard dated July 26, 1958:
The hon. member for St. Denis suggested we should retain files of people who apply for work in the Post Office Department. I would however point out to him that this is entirely the responsibility of the civil service commission. They recruit people and we are not in a position to do their work in any respect.
That amounts to saying that everything connected with the salaries and working conditions of postal employees is the responsibility of the civil service commission.
When the minister was sitting in the opposition, he used to complain that the morale of postal employees was rather low, and I quote what he said-because it is important that we understand what happened in the past and what is happening today. This is from page 7532 of Hansard for August 13, 1956:
No company organization and no government organization can operate successfully for very long if their employees do not have a high level of morale. When one reads the publication of the post office employees themselves and when one hears from time to time through the press of certain happenings across the country, one is led to wonder whether actually the morale among the staff of the post office in its entirety is as high as it should be. I rather doubt that it is. For that condition I lay the responsibility at the door of the government because of situations such as the one I outlined to you a few moments ago.
If we compare the morale of postal employees today with that prevailing at the time, we note there is a great difference; so I say that the minister now doubly deserves the criticism he was making as a private member. That criticism I take pleasure in returning to him, and I ask him, in turn, to try to improve the working conditions of the employees and to satisfy their requests.
For the last year or so, newspapers have been filled with criticism and protests from postal employees, and the minister's reply is always the same: "This is a matter for the civil service commission."

The minister will recall that, when he was in the opposition, he was scandalized because the Post Office Department showed an amount of $100,000 for travelling expenses. I am sorry I have to tell him this, but if we compare travelling expenses in 1957 with the current figure for his department, we find that in 1957 they amounted to $367,140, while in 1959 they reached $507,000. On telegrams and telephone calls, in 1957 the government spent $129,500; in 1960-1961 the estimates amount to $154,000, that is $25,000 more.
The minister is fond of publicity; he advertises all over the place: "Mail early", "Mail often", well, instead of gadding about, he should write; he would be saving money; let him heed his own publicity. If it is as good as he claims it is, why doesn't he use it himself? His trip to Paris would have cost him 10 cents instead of some larger amount that I am not aware of. Let him write letters.
Of course, he probably does not dare to write. In view of the criticism he has received about the poor design of stamps he has been issuing, maybe he is afraid of that kind of publicity. At any rate, I suggest that he use the mail more often, rather than the telephone or telegraph.
I suggest that he write often and early.
Usually, when we use the telephone or telegraph, it is because we have not foreseen what could happen.
For instance, when I telephone home it is because I forgot something. If I send a telegram, it is because the situation is urgent, and I have not foreseen what could happen. Therefore, the amounts of money spent for telephone calls and telegrams are expenses that could be cut substantially, which might help the Minister of Finance achieve a surplus next year. The latter could perhaps rely on the Postmaster General to do so.
As regards correspondence, however, he has no complaint, because he is very satisfied with the way correspondence is being done in his department. He even took great stock in the compliment paid to him by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. McFarlane), I believe, last year, to whom, according to the official record, he replied:

Mr. Chairman, I thank hon. members for their courtesy in allowing me additional time. I am also of the opinion that, like your humble servant, several hon. members know about this obsession of the Postmaster General's. To my mind, it is time we had at least one file concerning the Postmaster General, in which we might put information supplied by the minister and which we might pass along to the public. In fact, I shall take this opportunity of asking the minister if I may give my voters some information for which I asked on their behalf.
Mr. Chairman, all this is for the public relations division. I know that the Postmaster General is fond of publicity. In fact, I think he has been the most photographed Postmaster General since confederation. I have never seen him in public but he was accompanied by a photographer. I had the opportunity of accompanying him many times and I thank him for it. I felt very proud of it; and every time he asked me if I would be so kind as to have my picture taken with him I had no objection, but I think that his mania for publicity is exaggerated. As far as his department is concerned, I suggest that the public relations expenses apply more to the minister himself than to his department, and that this publicity angle is really carried too far.
For instance, why advertise that there is a Post Office Department in this country? Why publicize well known facts? There is no competition in this field. Everybody knows that to send a letter to some nearby city, one has only to use the mails. There is no need for all those publicity charges mentioned in the item now under review. To give you an example of the increase in departmental estimates, may I point out to the house that in 1957, publicity expenditures amounted to $207,500, while during the 1959-60 fiscal year, they reached $270,000, or an increase of

Supply-Post Office
$63,000. I suggest that those publicity expenditures could be reduced without affecting the department's efficiency.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to turn to another subject which the minister was very fond of taking up when he was in the opposition; I refer to patronage. He used to complain that the Liberal government indulged in patronage, and he said that even for the hiring of extra staff for the Christmas rush, no recommendations should be made by members of parliament, and the selection of applicants should be left to the department itself. Here were his words, as recorded in Hansard for August 13, 1956:
This is not the way to have the best possible government service. The best possible government service arises from allowing the departments freedom to choose their people without being influenced and without forcing applicants into obtaining recommendations from their members.
What has he done? He has set up a flying squad. I think he is fond of flights (robberies). I have asked him many questions about robberies that were committed, and heaven knows the department has not been too fortunate in that respect under his administration. He set up a so-called flying squad, which employs people regularly, on a part-time basis, people who are called on the telephone and asked to work at the post office. I asked him a certain question about that, and here is the reply I got from the minister:
(Text):
If the term "flying squad" refers to casual part time employees, the answer is yes. These casual employees are women who are called for work when there are sudden increases in mail volume in order to avoid delays and the necessity of working regular staffs overtime. These casual employees are generally called by telephone two or three hours before their services are required and usually work only one or two days a week for three or four hours on each occasion, depending on the volume of mail to be processed.
(Translation):
However, we find there have been 68 appointments since the present government took office. Most of those appointments were based on recommendations from Conservative members now sitting in the house and who were not here before 1957. If, as he has indicated, those hirings had been made "prior to July 1957", how does he explain that the names of Monteith, Benoit Gonthier, Pierre Sevigny, Valade, etc. are on the list of people who recommended flying squads?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: There are names of Liberal members too.

Yes, but only as window dressing. In fact, the Postmaster General was

kind enough to accept one, two, three, four and even five Liberal recommendations. But in view of his statement that people working for the Post Office Department should not be recommended by members of parliament, the minister's actions are contrary to what he preached when he was in the opposition. He told us those people worked three or four hours a day for two or three days a week. I have here a statement, which I got from a reliable source, to the effect that those people of the flying squad have worked 5 hours on April 27, 8 hours on April 29, 8 hours on May 2, 8 hours on May 3, and 8 hours on May 4. Therefore, when the minister says that those people worked a couple of days a week, two or three hours a day, I believe he is wrong and that he should see to it that the promises he made, when he was a private member, are fulfilled.
Those people take the place of casual employees, who have been hired for several years, perhaps also under recommendation of the minister, and who work but three or four hours each time, at the most; they are single women, or widows with or without children. The minister claims that those people are not interested because it is a temporary job. Now, these people, generally, work as casual employees because they need to work. They are widows, or elderly women who cannot get other jobs. If it is true that, from time to time, they change jobs, it is because they are not paid enough or because of their age or illness they have to quit.
I would say those flying squads are composed of people, most of the time recommended by the Conservatives, and that shows a disguised form of patronage. I would therefore ask him to have the matter looked into, in order that the regular employees, those who have passed their exams and who are on the waiting list may be treated more fairly. I respectfully submit that those flying squads set up by this government are causing an injustice to those who were successful in their examinations and who are waiting to be taken on the regular staff. We know that those people, if they are not called up for work during the year, after passing their exam, must take a new examination.
Therefore, people who are on those flying squads are filling jobs that could be filled by people who passed their test. So, these flying squads are detrimental to casual employees who have been working for years and who get employment for only three to

four hours at the most, while members of the flying squads, on the recommendation of our Conservative friends and the minister, get work for eight hours, not only once a week, but two or three times a week and even almost each day, as I indicated earlier.
I know that these casual employees are badly in need of work and that they would be glad to work six or seven hours a day; now they are told there is no more work for them. Here is what happens: their place is taken by those flying squads recommended by the Conservatives-

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
And
by the Liberals.
Yes, by one or two, to keep up appearances but the rest is made up of persons recommended by our Conservative friends from the province of Quebec.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
And
by some Liberals like Pit Lessard, Jean Paul Deschatelets, J. G. Ratelle, Senator Jodoin, Gerard Loiselle, Azellus Denis, Guy Rouleau.

Naturally, the Postmaster
General is intelligent, and has seen to it that two and even three friends of the Liberals are included in this list. But all those people have been hired with the mention "No recommendation". They certainly do not fall from heaven. Do you think for a moment that they have not been recommended by our friends? A phone call does not show on the file, and a letter marked "confidential" cannot be removed from the file. In fact, when the minister is asked about the recommendations in the files, the "personal and confidential" letters are not mentioned in the reports submitted to the house. If he has decided that there will be no patronage, there should not be any. In answer to a question asked by the hon. member for St. Jean-Iber-ville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) who wanted to know-
(Text):
Have there been any transfers of post offices in Canada since the month of June, 1957?
The answer was yes. Do hon. members know what the number of transfers actually was? It was 2,541.
(Translation):
On this list, there are 78 dismissals. There are resignations by the hundreds, and I readily believe-although I have not figured them out-that at least 500 of those changes are due to the partisanship of this government.
Let's not hear any more about Grit patronage.

Oh no.

speechtext: How many have you dismissed?

Mr. Chairman, we had been having peace since the beginning of my remarks; we had not yet heard the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard), and we were satisfied.
For my part, I thought he had gone to St. Hyacinthe-Bagot, to indulge in provincial politics, to busy himself with the big three, two of them dead, and the other one dying.
The years 1930 to 1935 were years under the Bennett regime, which was extolled if not by the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot, perhaps by his father or his predecessors. The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot very seldom refers to Mr. Bennett; I think he would rather just forget about him-so as I was saying, the things that were done under the Bennett government between 1930 and 1935 are being copied 100 per cent by the present government, which means that the present government will last no longer than five years. Coming back to what I was saying, between 1930 and 1935, the Tory government made 832 changes in the Post Office Department. Therefore, before raising cries of patronage against the Liberals, the hon. member should follow his own advice instead of dishing it out to others.
In his remarks earlier today, the minister referred to thefts. Do you know, Mr. Chairman, how many thefts there have been? The minister is lucky that the amount of the thefts has declined, but wait till next year and you will see an increase in both the number and the amounts of thefts.
The minister gives out the number and the amounts of thefts only when they are comparatively light. When the amounts are more significant, the minister deals with them in terms of percentage or average; and when they are too high, he even divides them by three. He always says, for instance, that the average is less now than at the time of the Liberals.
I have here the report of the Postmaster General himself, giving us an idea of the number and amounts of those thefts. Everybody is aware of it, and the Canadian people are aware of it. But, when one is as clever as the Postmaster General, everything is translated in small percentages and Canadians are given averages and proportional figures as an answer.
We see in the Potsmaster General's report, the number of thefts, receivings, irregularities, forgeries, etc.

Supply-Post Office
This is how the report reads. In 1957, the report mentions that there were 335 thefts and that the stolen amounts reached $110,500. In 1958, when we were already under the present administration, there were 355 thefts, and a stolen amount of $100,700.
Let me remind the house that the minister boasted last year that: "We had more thefts, but the amount of those thefts was much smaller".
Let us now look at the figures for 1959 in that respect. The number of thefts was 487. This is not the figure reported a few moments ago by the minister, when he said something that contradicts his own report. The number is 487.
Now, do you know the value of the stolen goods? It was $138,500, that is, an increase of $32,000 over 1957.
The minister cannot, therefore, contend that the amounts stolen were smaller. He even boasted that the then postmaster general was hiring thieves. Now, he will recall the recent robberies where employees themselves have stolen the contents of the trucks they were driving.
I think he might do well to read over again what he said on former occasions. He would be the happiest man in the world if the statements he made as a private member could be stamped "personal and confidential".
And what about the serious incidents that occurred recently? The latest important developments relate to the attitude shown by senior officials of his department who have been asking their subordinates to cheat-if I may use that word, which in fact is not too harsh -because in a circular, they instructed postmasters to accept as few American coins as possible, because at the bank, they would not get full value for it. As I say, they told the postmasters to accept as few U.S. coins as possible. Then they added, and I quote:
And if you accept any, try to pass it on to customers-*
-so that if there is any loss, it will be sustained by the customer, and not by the post office.
I see the minister shakes his head in denial. Let me read to him the circular on this point:
(Text):
A problem has arisen because of the volume of United States coins in circulation which have been accepted at par and on which a discount is now being charged by banks.

(Translation):
This is not what the minister said in the house, but it is what this circular states. And I continue:
(Text):
In view of this, the inclusion of United States coins in deposits or remittances should be kept to a minimum.
(Translation):
The circular does not tell postmasters to refuse U.S. coins and to accept only Canadian money. It says: accept as little as possible.
I continue:
(Text) :
Wherever possible, United States coins accepted at post offices should be handed out as change to other patrons.
(Translation):
That is one way of getting rid of something likely to bring about a deficit of some sort, because when this circular was being distributed, the banks were charging a certain discount on American coins.
I suggest that this procedure is not honest nor fair to post office patrons and I think that the Postmaster General should chastise the person responsible for the distribution of this circular instead of congratulating and commending that person as he did recently in the house. May I call it one o'clock?

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m. (Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take too much of the time of the house, because I understand it is the intention of the house to adopt the estimates of the Postmaster General as soon as possible. Although they are not encouraging, the minister enjoys such a majority in the house that, good or bad, his estimates will be adopted in any
case.

Mr. Chairman, before recess, I was dealing with the achievements of the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) who was boasting of achievements which belong exclusively to his subordinates and not to himself because, as far as the policy of the government is concerned, he will admit that to please the public and to say that such a policy has modernized and improved the situation, he must first say what that policy is.
When we hear the Postmaster General say he has ably administered his department, claiming he has had installed plastic letter boxes, I feel the people will not be content with such achievements, that they will rather want to know which promises he has now fulfilled that he made while sitting in the opposition. If the minister, who is intelligent, only thinks a little I doubt very much he will retain the confidence of his electors of Notre Dame de Grace, to whom he has so often promised two postal deliveries a day, and who have not yet obtained them after three years of administration.
I presume that at the time the minister did not expect to be appointed to that portfolio, and that the promises he was making had no importance whatever, because what was important for him was to be elected by making promises to his electors. However, I must pay him this tribute of having worked harder at getting elected than in running his department. In fact, as I said earlier, if he had tried as hard to get the world's fair for Canada as he did in getting elected, he would have started sooner and we could now be sure that the fair would be held in this country-
It is only because he did not want to be out or order.

Earlier today, the minister made a series of statements, but I have just learned that the text of his speech was sent yesterday to the members of the press gallery. I have a copy here and I see that it is a word for word reproduction of the comments made in this house by the Postmaster General. That is why we heard him make his speech with such fluency and without any mistake. I don't mean to say that he read his speech, but on seeing that this is a word for word transcript, we are a little inclined to suspect he did. However, in view of the importance of his department, I forgive him for giving to the house the exact wording of a speech which will no doubt be carried in tonight's papers.
The only thing lacking is the minister's picture; but as he is so fond of publicity, I
Supply-Post Office
assume that every newspaper has a copy of it, either with a scooter or something else, and I feel sure he will be given all the publicity he has personally prepared.
Mr. Chairman, I was therefore discussing the details of the electronic machines he calls his own, and which were initiated by the former Liberal government.
I think the Postmaster General will recognize that long before his assumption of the office of Postmaster General, consideration had been given to installing electronic machines to improve the department's efficiency, with this difference that previously he used to describe those machines as monsters that did not work, and that the money voted for such experiments was between $700,000 and $1 million. Now today, Mr. Chairman, we no longer know how much money is being spent by the Post Office Department on this equipment. However, I am sure it is over $3 million. Furthermore, it has been three years since the Postmaster General took over his department and was placed in charge of that famous $700,000 monster. How much money has been spent on the monster? What expenditures were authorized by the present Postmaster General to determine whether the various rented electronic machines should be retained in Canada, or should be thrown out?
In his report, the Postmaster General took credit for developments in the department for which minor officials and departmental heads are wholly responsible. I dealt with that matter earlier and there is no need to come back to it. He did not say what the cost will be of the electronic equipment experiments, but we should like to know. Is the minister able to tell us how many electronic machines are now on trial in the department and how many of them were imported? Government members used to be shocked because those electronic machines were not put in permanent use. How can the minister explain after three years in charge of this department, that we still do not know how many machines will be installed permanently and how many are rented?
I see in the Postmaster General's report that not only are we interested in the installation of electronic machines, but that electronic machines are rented from abroad on a trial basis. In other words, British electronic machines are being tested not in England but here in Canada, and we are paying rather substantial amounts for the renting and testing of those machines. I refer

Supply-Post Office
to Univac 120 which is imported from England and used here at a rental of $1,885 a month. I would like to know if a three-year period is not sufficient to decide if this electronic machine is to be accepted or if we should continue to rent it or buy it.
On the matter of departmental expenditures I would suggest to the minister that, as far as the rental of postal equipment is concerned, in 1956-57, at the time of the Liberal government, this expenditure was only $25,432, while in 1960 it will reach $97,750, that is an increase of about $75,000 a year.
Are we to continue to rent electronic equipment indefinitely, or are we finally going to instal them permanently?
The minister claims that this will not take the place of employees. And in a later statement he claims it will affect only those who are employed on a part-time basis. May I remind him that out of the 50,000 employees of his department, 28,000 are part-time employees. The minister has a habit of making statements one day that he hastily denies the next.
I would therefore ask him whether, when he shakes his head, he means no, or something else. As I was saying, over half the staff will be hit by automation. Will automation have any effect on Canada's 700,000 unemployed? Will applicants who passed examinations and are awaiting regular employment have to wait indefinitely because machines are taking their places? I think we should look twice before completely mechanizing the Post Office Department, and we should look into the cost, too. Never in the past has the Postmaster General revealed to the house the cost of the experiments conducted with those new electronic machines. We do not know, we are walking in a fog. We do not know whether those electronic machines cost millions, or whether they represent an economy for the postal service. I say to the minister that it is up to him to decide if experiments on this matter are to be suspended or if we shall keep on employing Canadian labour as usual until business revives and unemployment decreases.
I now come to another sort of mechanization, scooters. I know they are a sort of obsession with the minister, because he has often been photographed with a scooter.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: think you are jealous.

No I am not jealous, I would rather see him in the newspapers than in

person, because newspapers do not lie- whereas, in person, he is from time to time inclined to say things which are a bit removed from the truth, and from the things he advocated when he was sitting in the opposition. Now, Mr. Chairman, what do we know about the cost of those scooters? Do we know how many are being used? Have we been informed of the date when those tests with scooters will end?
He has made much of the fact he tried three-wheel and four-wheel scooters. But have we been told how much they cost? No. Garages are needed for these scooters. Those machines burn gas. We want to know whether postal employees require a driver's licence and who is paying for those licences. We want to know if a person who is hired as a letter-carrier has to have a driver's licence, etc. Those are details he should be giving us.
I wonder whether, instead of scooters, he has not also tried out ordinary tricycles, which are cheaper, easier to handle, and which would allow letter carriers to get closer to their points of call. Tricycles would also be easier to lock with a chain, for these scooters now in use remain in the street, motor running, and are liable to being stolen, as are other vehicles at the present time.
If the minister wants to make improvements, it would be a good idea, not only as he suggested himself but as was the practice when we had a well organized government to experiment with a cheaper method of mail delivery in suburban areas by having letter-carriers use bicycles. Then, he could tell us the cost of this experiment, and just when this service would be permanently provided in our country.
How many other promises did he make, Mr. Chairman, when he sat in the opposition, not with the intention of misleading the people but because he was convinced that such improvements were necessary. Then, why did he not carry them out?
I challenge the Postmaster General to tell me which of the promises he made while in the opposition have been fulfilled since he has taken office. There are none. Everyone remembers he wanted two deliveries a day. I remember the Postmaster General's question: When will we, in Notre Dame de Grace, have twice-daily mail deliveries? Will the people of his beautiful constituency of Notre Dame de Grace be favoured with two deliveries a day? I doubt it.
How can he come back before his people and say: I lied to you; I was wrong. I was

talking through my hat. I think I know how he will wriggle out of that one. Perhaps he has already thought of a way out.
There is one quality of his that I admire- he is a hard worker. He should apply his great skill for winning elections to running his department.
Furthermore, whenever he is designated to represent Canada abroad, for instance to determine where the world's fair is to be held, he should prepare for it in advance, so as not to be taken by surprise, and in that way he could produce results.
The minister spoke at length of the twice a day mail delivery, but he has no intention of having it written into the statutes of his department.
As far as stamps are concerned, I have dealt with the matter. Everybody knows what kind of stamps we have had these last few years. They have been criticized throughout the country. Yet, the minister cannot stand his stamps being criticized. He gives lectures, and those who do not like his stamps, just to quote his own words, are labelled "dry tongues".
But when you are dealing with someone who manages things like a school boy, who lacks seriousness, and takes the liberty of lectures on the way to stick a stamp, of making visits, and who introduces himself with the words: "I am a visitor, I am your Postmaster General, and I am pleased to come to Nova Scotia"; when you are dealing with a man who thinks himself a good Postmaster General in the eyes of the Canadian people, because he has set up plastic mail boxes, I think we are entitled to tell him that he himself is a joker.
When, in philatelic exhibitions, we find stamps commemorating ancient battles which took place in Canada, in 1700 and even in 1600, between the English and the French, when everybody is looking for peace, we can say, I think, that the choice is in bad taste and that the minister should be more discriminating.
Printing costs for those stamps should be lowered. I would point out to the minister that those printing costs are not acceptable and that there should be some attempt at saving in that field.
As a matter of fact, the government of which the minister is a member, follows an economic policy of deficits and a cut in printing costs for stamps is called for.
As a matter of fact, the Post Office Department spent $686,000, in 1956, whereas today, it is spending $927,000.
