No, Mr. Chairman, I was pointing out that the stamp itself has nothing to do with the printing cost, and if the minister wants to argue on the basis that the population is rising, I say it is a weak argument, Of course there are more people in Canada, as he says.
If he used postage meters to eliminate stamp printing costs, as suggested last week, I think he could save money.
Another promise had to do with postal savings banks. The postal banks have been competing with commercial banks. I think the Postmaster General will recall having stated that the former minister had no right to set up postal banks, because such a system competed with commercial banks and was unnecessary.
What did he do? Not only did he increase their number, but he encouraged that increase by raising the rate of interest payable to depositors.
Therefore, he did not abolish savings banks, but created more. There are 37 more. Either he was wrong at the time, or else he is wrong now.
Another promise made by the minister concerns the R.C.M.P., which was supposed to take over all security arrangements of the postal department.
Was that done, Mr. Chairman? No. Today, the minister says-and that is his reply- that the provincial police, in the various provinces, looks after the problem.
Now that problem existed at the time. When the minister was a private member he knew very well that there was such a thing as provincial police.
Why tell the people of Canada that if the Conservative government took office the R.C.M.P. would look after the security of the Post Office Department?
That is another promise which has not been fulfilled, another statement made by the minister to win an election. Nothing has been done since he has taken office.
I think the minister should mind his department more, as far as the policy of the government is concerned and I think he should not boast about routine matters that come exclusively under the jurisdiction of civil servants, to whom I should like once again to pay tribute. He should stop boast-

Supply-Post Office
ing at the expense of his own officials, to whom he has refused salary increases and to whom he is now denying better working conditions.
Today, much is being said about obscene publications, about advertising sent out through the mail.
I have here a letter which the minister must have received-because it was addressed to him-from Mr. Dennison, a member of the board of control of the city of Toronto.
(Text):
-the controller, Mr. Dennison, from the city of Toronto, and I want to read part of it:
I enclose printed material together with money-back guarantee directed to me by mail, which has been described by the better business bureau as a "phony".
Then a little farther down:
I think the Canadian government should take steps comparable to those of the American government to prevent the use of the mails for this type of fraudulent advertising and promotion. This company should be required to prove the validity of their claims before they are permitted to use the mails as a means of extracting from Canadians hundreds of thousands of dollars through this fraudulent advertising campaign.
(Translation):
Did the minister do anything to prevent the Canadian people from being misled by advertisements that are more or less senseless and which are condemned by the Better Business Bureaux? It was a civic-minded individual who wrote the minister on this matter, namely, Mr. William Dennison, commissioner of the city of Toronto.
Mr. Chairman, it is not the responsibility of a Toronto commissioner to hear those complaints and to remedy the situation. It is the exclusive responsibility of the Postmaster General and he should inform us of the answer he gave to this controller so that the Post Office Department should not be used for the distribution of obscene literature and fraudulent advertising.
Mr. Chairman, I had promised the Postmaster General that he could go back home in peace after the adoption of his estimates. Besides, government members are in the majority in this house.
I conclude my remarks by saying that, during his three years at the helm of the Post Office Department, the minister has kept none of the dozens of promises he had made. In view of his administration, of his past statements and his present attitude, we could hold a Canadian fair right here, even if we did not succeed in his efforts to bring the world fair to Canada.

So, I suggest that we could have a fair in this country to exhibit all the promises and achievements of the Postmaster General. For instance, we could have an exhibit showing the way to have a world fair. We could also have an exhibit of a "personal and confidential" correspondence system "a la Hamilton".
We could exhibit a collection of exclusive, unusual, bad and ill-designed stamps.
We could also have an exhibit showing the R.C.M.P. working for the Post Office Department.
We could have a chart of the Postmaster General's thrift, the ideal financial administration indicated by deficits. The Canadian postal service, haven of underpaid employees. The savings funds checked by the government. The $1 million electronic monster changed into a $3 million one.
We could also indicate the elimination of wastefulness, the controversial stamp issues, the increase of postal services by a decrease of post offices, because, since last year, 116 post offices have been shut down. The cutting down of thefts through their increase. The twice-daily delivery in Notre Dame de Grace. Patronage under the guise of flying squads. Conflict between the department's public relations and the minister's personal publicity. The smuggling of American coins. Letter carriers astride scooters.
Mr. Chairman, I ask once again that the minister reply to all the questions that we have put to him. We would like to know the details of government policy. We are not interested in knowing that his officials have done well because they are worthy of praise, but how the present Postmaster General, since his appointment to his important duties, has promoted the policy of that department, because we want to be better informed and learn something else than the mere fact that the government has installed plastic postal boxes throughout the country.
(Text):

Mr. Chairman, on behalf of the political group I represent I would like to pay our respects, our compliments and our commendations to all the many tens of thousands of Canadians who are concerned in all these services rendered to us by the post office. I should personally like to express my appreciation to the minister for the prompt manner in which he has always undertaken to look into and to investigate each and every complaint or recommendation that I have made during the past year. We would especially like to extend our best wishes to the

newly appointed parliamentary secretary and we hope that his able services are going to enable the minister to pay even closer attention to the representations that we make.
The post office, Mr. Chairman, is an institution that in the main we regard as one of the most efficient in the Dominion of Canada. It is accepted as a necessary publicly owned institution by all parties in this house. Before any institution can be successfully publicly owned there must be established in the hearts and minds of all employees of that institution a feeling of pride and also a feeling of ownership in the institution; otherwise you will not have efficiency at its maximum when such a large enterprise is owned by the taxpayers as a whole. We are very pleased to note that almost without exception the employees of our post office regard their work with a high level of pride and realize that they are rendering a very necessary and much appreciated public service.
I feel that on taking up the estimates of the Postmaster General there is absolutely no need for partisanship. It is an institution the need of which we all recognize, and I see no cause for a party spokesman aiming to take political advantage of whatever weaknesses arise from time to time, because the larger the institution, very often the larger are the weaknesses to be found.
I find it very hard, therefore, to agree with the minister's conclusion in his report this morning that postal services are getting hard to improve. I feel that this will likely never be the case and I think the minister is being unduly optimistic when he expects there is very little which can be done to improve postal services.
I should like to call the minister's attention in the first place to the financial aspect. We are not opposed to the post office operating at a loss if that is necessary. I notice that since the minister has become minister he has now reported an operating loss for each of two succeeding years. I also noticed his statement that he hoped that this year he would have, I believe he said, a miserable $1.7 million of revenue in excess of expenditure. We all hope that the minister's expectations will be realized but I hope it will not be at the expense of a raise in wages of the employees to enable this expectation to become reality.
However, I feel that much of the subsidization of the postal services is not correctly represented in that the operating report does not include the cost of buildings and the depreciation thereon, which cost is borne
Supply-Post Office
by the Department of Public Works. When the minister replies I wish he would supply us with an estimate of how much more this deficit would have been had his department had the financial responsibility of putting up the buildings, with their consequent depreciation and upkeep. I believe when he supplies that answer we will realize that our post office as a department has never really made money for the taxpayers of Canada but has always on balance been an expense.
We hope very much that the employees of the post office will not have to help the minister in his endeavours to arrive at a net profit for the year by being asked to work at below average wage levels. I believe one other hon. member intends to speak in more detail on this matter so I am going only to say this. The minister underlined in his report that in the postal department there has been the lowest turnover of personnel among all employees of any government department. I think that is what the hon. gentleman said. Thereby, I believe, he attempted to indicate that morale was at a relatively high level. It is my opinion that among all civil servants the employees of the Post Office Department have about the lowest morale.
In all the meetings held last year after that black announcement of the Minister of Finance regarding civil service wages, the most annoyed of all the civil servants and the ones most anxious to take aggressive action in order to pursue their demands were the employees of the minister's department, and I believe the same situation prevails now.
My main reason for speaking today is to do what I can, in my humble way, to persuade the minister of the truth of my contention that efficiency in business is not necessarily enhanced by enlarging its size. There is a fundamental law of economics referred to as the law of diminishing returns, and I believe that when a post office begins to serve more than, roughly, a population of 100,000 the point of maximum return has been reached. Thereafter, inefficiency begins to enter into the picture to a growing degree.
Ever since the end of the last war we have noticed a tendency for the officials responsible for administering the postal service in our larger urban areas to express a desire to take over post offices in the smaller communities around those urban areas, to absorb them. The minister mentioned in his report that more and more post offices have been opened within the last year. I notice, however, in his latest annual report, at page 31, that in Canada on March 31, 1958 there were in

Supply-Post Office
operation 11,768 post offices. One year later, on March 31, 1959 there were in operation only 11,634. The number of new post offices established in that year total 116. However, the number of post offices which were closed amounted to 250, and we ended the year, not with more post offices to serve the needs of the people of Canada but with 134 less.
I realize that there are circumstances where the retention of certain post offices may no longer be worth while, and I do not want to condemn the department at all for locking up maybe half of these 250 post offices that were locked up. However, I feel that many of these offices were closed in order to enlarge the operations of urban post offices which had already exceeded their peak of efficiency in relation to size. I know that if you are a postmaster in a town, and you are classified as a grade 13 postmaster, for instance, it is very nice if you can persuade the administration to allow you to take in a number of surrounding post offices and place them under your jurisdiction. As a result, you might no longer be a grade 13 postmaster; you might become a grade 15 postmaster.
Our urban areas are growing rapidly, however, and I see no need of this process. I think the employees of the post office, especially the postmasters and the superintendents together with all the hierarchy of the post office should be prepared to wait for an improvement in their classification as the population of Canada grows within their respective areas. They should not advance themselves at the expense of surrounding post offices. I think that practice is very unfair to the suburban communities involved, and it is also unfair to the employees concerned, because they are very often handicapped after such a procedure has been undertaken.
The people in the southern area of Vancouver-those I know of, at least, and this may also be the case elsewhere-definitely feel that poorer service has resulted. These are not complaints from my political supporters. These are complaints which I receive each and every week end I spend at home. I can talk to my local bank manager or to the local lumber operator; I can speak to almost anyone engaged in business, and they all complain loud and long about the rapid deterioration of postal service that has taken place since these amalgamations have taken effect. Either measures will have to be undertaken to improve the service, or the department will have to pay attention to a process of decentralization of the existing service.
I know we have that monstrous new post office in the city of Vancouver, including a $2 million underground tunnel leading to the
IMr. Regier.]
C.P.R. station. What a horrible blunder that was in the annals of the Canadian post office, as I think the minister will readily agree.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Would the hon. member date the time that was decided on, please?

Yes. In order to keep the record right, this was decided on in the days of the Liberal government. We have a C.N.R. station and we also have a C.P.R. station. They decided to build one $2 million underground tunnel to connect the nearest railway station, if you please, to the post office. Five per cent interest on that $2 million would be sufficient to supply enough money to build one new $100,000 post office in the surrounding communities each and every year. In any case, the tunnel is not adequately used, because as everyone knows practically all first class mail comes in by air today, so the tunnel is only made use of to haul the newspapers and the advertising garbage that pours in. I hope errors of this kind and especially of this magnitude will not be repeated by the Canadian Post Office Department.
I should like to see the Post Office Department make a greater effort with regard to paying attention to municipal boundaries. I know that the orthodox reply one receives on making representations to this effect is that post offices simply cannot pay attention to municipal boundaries. I feel, however, that that is a wrong position to take. I will admit that the department cannot always pay attention to municipal boundaries. Whenever possible, however, the post office should make a policy to respect municipal boundaries. The city of Port Moody, for instance, should not have to receive one third of its mail via New Westminster while the other two thirds is handled in Port Moody. This is the situation in many other towns in Canada. I think that instead of relying on a principle laid down by some official many long years ago, the department ought to have another look at this thing to see whether a little more attention could not be paid to the interests of the communities concerned.
I would like the minister to explain why the progress made in building new post offices is so slow. I am afraid that in 1960 the number of starts may be less than the number in 1959. In the departmental report for the year ending March 31, 1959 the minister claims that in the preceding year 65 new buildings were completed. We have a total of 11,634 post offices in Canada. If we are prepared to build only 65 new buildings a year that indicates on the basis of my arithmetic that the government expects post office buildings to last roughly 200 years. That

is an odd rate of depreciation at this time when there is so much unemployment. I believe we should build at least 165 new buildings a year.
The condition of post offices in many parts of Canada is a disgrace to the federal government. It is time we embarked on a more ambitious program in this regard instead of curtailing our program to meet the aims of the Minister of Finance. I hope the construction of no necessary post office has been delayed because in the opinion of the government this is the year in which it had to arrive at a balanced budget.
Other hon. members in this group will say something about twice a day delivery as being necessary to the business community and a source of additional employment.
Would the minister tell us if in the larger urban areas wickets remain closed after a certain hour? If it is not the policy in Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg and Vancouver to have one wicket open around the clock, Sundays and holidays included, it should be. It is unreasonable to expect large urban areas to be served by post offices with wickets that close at five thirty or six o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman keep that open all night or until 2 a.m.?

In Vancouver the demand would be great enough for one wicket to be open all night and the same would hold true for Montreal. There are many people in the modern business world today who have a need for postal services at odd hours of the day and night. Arrangements could easily be made for around the clock service and it would be in the public interest if this were done.
The requirement for door to door delivery in towns should be lowered. The required population for this service should be reduced by 50 per cent. People today no longer like to walk a number of miles to get their mail at the local post office. We have many growing smaller towns which could have this service if the requirement were lowered.
I often wonder why the operations of the post office savings bank could not be combined advantageously for both the people of Canada and the Minister of Finance with the annuities branch of the Department of Labour. They could operate as one unit. I regret that the balance on deposit at the beginning of the fiscal year continues to show a decline. There has been a constant decline from $39 million on deposit in 1954 to $34 million in 1959. Since 1954 there has even been a slight decline in the number of post office savings banks in existence. Only one
Supply-Post Office
out of every eight post offices in Canada offers this service. The objects of the service are to encourage people to save and to enable the government to use the savings of the Canadian people in the public interest while paying only a modest rate of interest. The money now on deposit enables the government to have a considerable amount in interest rates each year.
The Minister of Finance pays 5 per cent when he borrows money and he paid over 6 per cent last year. I do not know what interest is paid on the money deposited in the post office savings bank but I believe it is not in excess of 3 per cent and perhaps it is even lower. The minister might inform us about that.
The hon. member for St. Denis referred to the advertising expenditures of the minister. I recommend that some of the advertising revenue available to the minister be diverted to more adequately informing Canadians of the availability of the post office savings bank. It is very much in the public interest at this time that people be encouraged to save. It is also important that the Minister of Finance receive as much investment money as he can at the lowest possible rate of interest. This is an excellent medium of making money available to the government.
On the whole we are proud of the operations of the Post Office Department and its employees and officials. However, we are unable to agree with the minister that it is becoming difficult to improve. The financial aspects of the department could be improved. It could be put on a more self-sustaining basis than now. I plead with the minister to occasionally ignore the advice of some of his leading officials who urge the construction of larger post offices at the expense of the smaller surrounding communities. We hope he will adopt the attitude of the former minister of public works who expressed the feeling that bigness is not synonymous with efficiency and who lent a considerable hand in increasing the construction of new post offices in smaller communities.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to commend the Postmaster General on his efforts to improve the postal services of Canada and also to thank him for the personal interest which he has shown in certain individual matters which I have brought to his attention.
Before going on to some further matters which I wish to draw to his attention I should like to pay tribute to the staff of his department, particularly to the administrative staff both here and in my province. I do not think there are any more conscientious or

Supply-Post Office
dedicated public servants to be found in any government department than can be found in the Post Office Department.
Newfoundland has peculiar problems with respect to mail services and the success with which those problems have been overcome and the improvements which have been carried out are due in no small measure to the efforts and the calibre of the people in the administrative part of the Post Office Department in our province.
Personally, 1 want to tell the minister that I have received every co-operation possible, and all my problems have always been given very sympathetic consideration. The new post office which was opened in St. John's recently has contributed greatly to the convenience of the public and also to the improvement of the working conditions of the staff. In addition, it has made for more efficient supervision and administration.
There is room, I think, for some revision of policy in connection with the classification of post offices. I draw a distinction between the classification of postmasters and post offices. There was a time when the salary of postmasters depended upon the revenue of the post office itself. I believe that has changed now and a better basis has been found, which takes into account not only the stamps sold but the other duties which have to be performed, the pieces of mail handled, and so on, but the classification of the post office itself still rests, I think, on the basis of revenue. In my province this gives rise to some very peculiar problems.
In my own riding most of the post offices- practically 90 per cent of them-are small revenue post offices where the services of the Post Office Department and those of the Canadian National Telegraphs are carried out by the same employee. I have drawn attention to this on previous occasions and I had hoped that something would have been done before this because there is a special problem in respect of Newfoundland arising out of the difficulty in relating our previous policy before confederation to that of the federal government.
Prior to confederation it was the practice to build separate post offices in communities where it was felt they would be a greater convenience to the people. The places where those post offices were built had no relation whatever to the size of the place or to the revenue of the place, although in most cases they were built in the larger fishing settlements. Now the federal Post Office Department will erect separate buildings for post offices only when the revenue reaches a certain figure. But since it acquired those buildings which had already been erected prior

to confederation and has carried out the policy of repairing and replacing them when necessary, we now have a situation where a very small community may have a separate post office building, while a much larger community is not able to get one.
In communities where the population is around 300, 400, or 500 people it is not convenient to have a post office in somebody's residence; it is not convenient for the people in a one hundred family settlement to have to go to somebody's back porch to mail a letter or to line up and get their mail. I think something should be done to alleviate this problem and to eliminate the seeming discrimination between those settlements which were lucky enough to get a separate postal building before confederation and those which have now grown larger and more important but are still not able to qualify under the present policy of the government.
As I said before, this is a special problem in Newfoundland, and I think it deserves special consideration and special treatment. I am not at all sure that the present policy of the Post Office Department in putting the onus upon the postmaster to find accommodation for the post office is a good one or a fair one. It seems to me to be putting an unnecessary burden on the postmaster and it makes for discrimination between a postmaster in one settlement where such accommodation can be found easily and cheaply and the postmaster in another settlement where he would have to go to the expense of putting up a building himself. I know the fact that this allowance is rated as salary and since it will perhaps help the postmaster to get a little better pension on retirement it may look like an advantage, but looking at the over-all picture I believe it is not a satisfactory policy. Not only is it not fair to the postmaster himself but it is not fair to the public because the people in one community have the right to expect the same type of service that they can find in another community of similar size.
The Postmaster General will not expect me to sit down without saying something about the postmaster-telegrapher problem. I am not going to repeat what I have said on previous occasions because since I raised this problem here in parliament the Postmaster General himself has had an opportunity to go to my province and to get firsthand knowledge of this problem; but I do want to tell him that there are still many cases where an injustice exists. I am a firm believer in putting right whatever needs to be put right and if we cannot put everything right, then we should put right as much as we can, and there are still some cases arising

out of this situation which have gone on now for 10 years and are still getting worse instead of better.
I still want to impress upon the Postmaster General that I consider his department has a moral obligation to do something about those people because it was his department which entered into the agreement which brought this situation about.
I should also like to say a few words about the handling of mail. The minister has emphasized that there is not much room for further improvement as far as internal arrangements are concerned but there is certainly room for improvement in the handling of mail. 1 know it has been my experience quite often to receive publications, magazines and papers through the mail which have been mutilated in transit. Once in a while we have the experience of receiving a parcel which has been crushed or broken while passing through the mail.
I happened to be in Montreal one day about a year ago and while proceeding from St. Catherine street to the C.N.R. station I passed along a street where one of the Montreal post offices is located. I would not have noticed the incident except that while I was walking down the street a truck backed up across the street in front of me and I saw the driver pick up bags of mail and throw them from a high platform right onto the truck, a distance of some 30 or 40 feet. With treatment of that sort any kind of fragile parcel in a mail bag would be damaged.
I do not know what safeguards the minister can take to prevent that sort of thing happening but I can assure him that it does happen because I have seen it myself. I believe that some measures should be taken to reduce such rough handling of the mail to the absolute minimum.
The question of broken or damaged parcels brings up the matter of insurance. When the minister replies to the remarks that have been made I wish he would be good enough to tell us something about the conditions under which insurance can be collected for a broken parcel. I know of a case where an electric razor was sent through the mail and when it arrived the outside case had been broken and it was in a very damaged condition. When the person applied for compensation on his insured parcel he was unable to collect. I am not clear on just what grounds he was refused but I know that he was refused although he could provide evidence that the damage had occurred while the parcel was passing through the mail.
Before resuming my seat there is one small matter I should like to bring to the attention of the Postmaster General. It has to do with
79951-0-271
Supply-Post Office
notices as to the forwarding of mail. When a person moves from one postal address to another I understand that if he wants his mail forwarded he fills out a little card advising the post office where his mail is to be sent. But these cards are only good for three months, and in the case of people like myself who have to be in Ottawa for six or eight months it often happens that we forget the card is good for only three months and several weeks' mail will pile up at the old address without being forwarded. I do not think it would be asking too much of the Postmaster General if he would arrange to have a reminder sent from the post office indicating that the period has expired and asking for further instructions.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure that members of the committee were very interested in hearing some of the advances that are being made in the Post Office Department as outlined by the minister this morning. I particularly noticed that he used words such as automation, mechanization and electronic equipment. These are terms that are causing a good deal of concern to labour across the country at the present time and these matters have received the attention of the house on several occasions. There is no doubt that they constitute a very important problem.
Could the minister outline what studies he has made into the long term effect of automation in the Post Office Department, particularly what effect it is going to have on the staff? I think such a study could be very useful to parliament because here we have a very large government department faced with a problem that is confronting industry generally throughout the country. It seems to me we have an opportunity here to have a firsthand study of the effects of automation on the staff of a government department. I would ask the minister to outline what is being done with respect to studying the problem. I know he has told us that there is going to be no great disruption of employment in the department because of automation but perhaps he could go a little further and give us a general outline of what study has been made in that regard. I am sure it would be helpful to the committee.

Mr. Chairman, there are two or three matters I should like to raise under item No. 1 of the Postmaster General's estimates. May I first add a few words to the comments made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam with relation to the employees of the minister's department. I feel quite certain that all members of the committee will agree that in the vast majority

Royal Assent
of cases employees throughout the civil service are most efficient and loyal. There is no question about that whatsoever. But I want to emphasize particularly that I do not think there is a more loyal group of civil servants, who at the same time have had less attention, than those in the Post Office Department.
I refer particularly to the postal clerks and even more so to the letter carriers, a group of civil servants whose work is outside 99 per cent of the time. They have to start very early in the morning and carry heavy loads under varying weather conditions. If ever a medal were cast by the government of Canada for people who have to face problems I think it should be presented to the letter carriers because they render the highest degree of service that can be expected of any man.
I am rather upset that the postal clerks and especially the postal carriers have so far not been among those classifications that have received an increase in remuneration. I sincerely hope that the Postmaster General-

Before we were called to proceed to the other place I was coming to the last sentence of what I had to say on the first point I raised in connection with the first item of these estimates. I will not repeat what I said previously, but merely conclude that section of my remarks by expressing the hope that the Postmaster General will use his position and influence to see that the postal clerks and the postal employees receive an increase in remuneration as speedily as possible, and that it be made retroactive to the first date upon which an increase was given to any civil servant during this session of parliament.

The second point I wish to raise is one in connection with which I admit I have not the fullest information. Her Majesty's mails are most important and I understand it is possible to send almost anything one wishes through the mails with the assurance of delivery. It is my understanding that for a long time it has been a growing practice among banking concerns to use the services of the post office either within a city or between adjoining cities for the purpose of transferring money, sums running into thousands of dollars or even hundreds of thousands of dollar. I am given to understand that this places a great burden upon the Post Office Department which the department was not originally intended to bear. If my information is correct, there are robberies upon occasions-and I am not referring to them in the same sense as the hon. member for St. Denis-but though the sums transmitted are covered by insurance I understand the banks do not put in claims. That is my understanding. I do know that in the past year or two there has been an upsurge in robberies of banks and post offices, as a result of which the department has had to take additional measures for its protection, and so forth.
I should like to hear from the Postmaster General whether he does feel that in principle it is the responsibility of the Post Office Department to accept huge amounts of money for transfer between banks either in the same city or in adjoining cities, and whether this matter has been taken up with the banks, possibly with a view to telling them that in the circumstances it would be only right for them to remove this burden from the post offices of our country and make other arrangements, perhaps with Brinks, to take care of this work. I should very much like to hear whether any consideration is being given to this question, whether there has been any consultation with the banks along these lines and whether any decision has been reached or, indeed, can be reached with the banks on this matter.
On the third point I wish to raise, we would appreciate hearing very much what consideration is being given by the Postmaster General to the costing of the services which are supplied by his department. We appreciated very much the information which was given to the committee by the Postmaster General when he introduced his estimates this morning. This question of costing is not a new one as far as I am concerned. I have been interested in it during the seven years I have had the honour of being a member of this house. I have spoken about it on more than one occasion in this chamber 79951-0-271J
Supply-Post Office
and also in the estimates committee when the estimates of the Post Office Department were before that committee two or three years ago. The postal service is a public service and it is under public ownership. I cannot understand why the policy of this and previous governments has been that a public service should subsidize commercial private enterprise. A question was put to the Postmaster General as reported at page 1641 of Hansard of March 2, 1960 in reply to which he stated that during the fiscal year 1958-59 the estimated excess of disbursements over receipts amounted to $21,690,000 for newspapers and periodicals.
I have briefly examined the information supplied by the minister this morning. In 1958-59 the Post Office Department handled 1,943,798,566 pieces of first class ordinary mail at a profit of 1.827 cents per piece. In that period it handled 844,443 pieces of domestic air mail at a profit of 17.665 cents per piece. It handled in that period 294,261,801 pieces of third class householder mail and 823,694,834 pieces of third class addressed circulars at a profit of .013 and .183 cents per piece respectively. Only in those services was the revenue greater than the expenditure. We can understand a loss on a public service such as money orders, notched and denominative and on special delivery mail, etc. But why should first class ordinary mail across Canada or domestic air mail have to assume what I maintain is a subsidy to private commercial firms?
On second class transient mail there was a loss of 9.339 cents per piece and on second class publishers' mail there was a loss of 4.084 cents per piece during the period 1958-59. Those who put magazines or newspapers through the mail are in a commercial business. Those who have what are usually called throw-aways are in the advertising business. Why should those who send first class mail be expected to subsidize those engaged in profit-making businesses of a commercial nature?
In 1951, two years before I came here, when there was some thought of changes being made in postal rates the Canadian Daily Newspaper Publishers Association protested the increase on grounds referred to by the minister in an answer reported at page 1675 of Hansard of March 2, 1960:
the proposed rates of postage would make it necessary for the publishers to charge a higher subscription price.
Surely it was not the intention that the post office as a public service should subsidize private commercial operations. When changes in the postal rates were last debated in this chamber the proposed increase on

Supply-Post Office
first class mail was such as to more than cover the loss on second and third class mail. Having heard the present Postmaster General and other hon. members of the cabinet speak on the subject when they were in opposition, we expected that a new evaluation might take place of the policies of the department, that for service rendered you shall pay. I thought that was a principle of free enterprise. It certainly is a principle of socialism.
The department made a profit in the past and now it has a deficit. A deficit is made up from the public purse. Perhaps the minister would tell us what studies have been or are being made on the question of the costing of the revenues and expenditures in connection with services rendered and in particular on the subsidy being paid by the average citizen on first class mail to advertisers, publishers and newspapers.
When the minister speaks will he tell us, clearly, honestly and bluntly, if he believes that private commercial enterprise should be subsidized by Canadian taxpayers in the event of a deficit in his department or by the users of first class mail? There is a principle involved and we are interested in hearing the viewpoint of the Postmaster General.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps at this point I could attempt to deal with some of the observations made during the course of this morning and afternoon and answer as quickly as possible some of the questions raised.
First, I would like to say this. Hon. members have charged me with saying in effect that there is little room for improvement in the post office. Now, this is a quick misinterpretation of something I said today. What I really said was-and I think this is the quotation-"We are still trying to improve, but it is getting harder". I pointed that out because of the fact that only one one hundredth of one per cent of our mail now results in inquiries or complaints and, therefore, if we are going to improve, we have to work on that one one hundredth of one per cent of the mail volume.
The first statement to which I take exception is that I implied that there was little room for improvement in our administration. That is the sort of self-satisfaction that I do not permit myself or my department to indulge in.
I will deal first with the remarks of the hon. member for St. Denis, Mr. Chairman, made during his speech of one hour and 35 minutes. I checked that for basis of comparison a few minutes ago while you were in the other place, Mr. Chairman. I was interested to see that he occupied more time

speaking on my estimates this year than he did in all of his efforts in the 22 years that he sat on the government side of the house.
Cheap stuff.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
In
his opening remarks he said he felt there was a lack of success as far as the Post Office Department was concerned. I am not going to deal with that. I shall let my remarks which are on the record as to the things which have been done this year in the Post Office Department speak for themselves and refute that observation.
He said I am a Postmaster General-
Dealing with deficits.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
He
said that I am a Postmaster General who believes in deficits. If he had listened to my remarks and had understood them, if he was listening, he would have found that in the year ended March 31, I960 we had a surplus of $1.7 million. It rather seems to me that a man who attempts for over an hour and a half to criticize the Post Office Department and does not know the difference between a surplus and a deficit is on rather weak ground in this field.
I should make this point very definitely. The basic philosophy of the department, as far as I am concerned, is to attempt to equate our revenue and our expenditures and to come out somewhere near even. Two years ago, in the first year under the administration of this department, our loss was $400,000. In 1958-59 it was just under $200,000. This year it is a surplus of $1.7 million, and when you are dealing with a total of almost $200 million you cannot come much closer to perfection.
The hon. member for St. Denis said that all our improvements are the responsibility of the deputy and the post office officials. I am not going to debate that with him at all. What I do say is that a reasonable portion of that which is going on in the department is the result of ideas which I have myself acquired in thinking about our problems and in my trips going around the country.
Which ones?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
But
we work together as a team, and this is the important thing. I am not interested in debating who gets credit for what; I am only interested in giving this country the best possible postal service it has ever had.
The hon. member said I gave no details about the cost of anything new. He should have learned in his 25 years in the house that on your opening speech you give the general picture and then you proceed

to deal with details as they are required by the hon. members. To give an example of just the sort of thing he would have had me doing, he said, "You did not give any details about the mailmobiles". I have them here, the results of an official survey to determine our progress. The direct costs for the period April, 1959 to February 29, 1960, including chauffeur and vehicle licence, gasoline, oil, greasing, repairs, tires, storage and depreciation totalled $4,129.75. Direct savings through the elimination of certain parcel post and relay bundle deliveries, $2,545.32, and net savings in transportation, letter carriers, $650.40, for a total direct savings of $3,195.72, and indirect savings representing the salary of one letter carrier and additional relief on annual leave and on rotation days, $3,288.65, for a total savings of $6,484.37, as against a total cost of $4,129.75, or a net saving of $2,354.62. This experiment involved five mailmobile routes covering an area formerly served by six foot walks.
If the committee had thought this was the kind of thing I was going to put in my original statement without being asked the specific areas in which they were interested, may I say it was not my intention to burden it with such detail unless requested.
To continue with the remarks of the hon. member for St. Denis, he charged me with taking responsibility for salaries and working conditions of everybody in the post office. This is primarily the function of the civil service commission and the Minister of Finance. What I do take credit for, and what is our proper responsibility, are the regulations and the operating conditions under which our employees work and the relations, in so far as they exist-and there is an extensive area in which they do-between management and staff in the post office. In those areas, we have made progress, and those relations have been improved.
The hon. member for St. Denis referred to travel expenses and said they have gone up. The results are reflected in the drop in our inquiries and complaints and in improvements of service because in the last two or three years we have given much more adequate supervision in the field. In order to achieve this better service we have more area superintendents who are responsible for getting out and directly supervising activities in our post offices and we have a far greater degree of collaboration between our headquarters and the field. I am urging our headquarters officials all the time to get out to the field and supervise what is going on and know what is going on so that they come back with the information to improve service.
Supply-Post Office
The hon. member complained about the fact that I have sent out a letter to members giving them information on the way in which they could contact senior officials of my department in case they wanted information. He omitted to quote from that letter the following sentence:
It is not my intention to create the thought that you should not let me know of your problems, but simply that I realize that you may wish to get detailed facts or to talk over a situation directly with the official who has been previously handling the actual case.
I am delighted to have members come to me with their problems-unlike the previous administration, which tried to sweep everything under the rug; I know this because I encountered difficulty myself as a member in direct dealing with officials of the department. My predecessors wanted everything to go through the minister. It is my view that there should be access, and direct access, between hon. members of this house and officials of the department so that they can get information easily and efficiently.
The hon. member mentioned a letter in which there had been a delay of two months, I think it was, between his sending it and my reply. This is an unusual case, as he will agree. He came to me for the information he would have been told it was in regard to a piece of third class mail coming from the United States and that it was necessary, therefore, for me to write to the United States and obtain this information, and that was where the delay occurred, as he knows very well.
Then he referred to an exaggerated desire for publicity on my part. I think I may assume that it is not my fault that previous postmasters general have sat here in Ottawa or have been engaged in activities other than those of the post office. In the work that I have done I have travelled across this country to visit post offices and find out what is going on and people report those activities from time to time. I just want you to know it is easier to find me in a post office than on a golf course.
Let me return to the mailmobile for a moment. The hon. member raised the objection with respect to the mailmobile that we did not give adequate consideration to Canadian manufacture. The short answer to that is that we started with a United States item only because after canvassing 18 possible Canadian manufacturers we could not find one who had anything that would come anywhere near fitting our requirements. After they were in operation here in Canada and Canadian manufacturers had a chance to look at them they began to develop something which was suitable for our purpose.

Supply-Post Office
We are now trying out a Canadian machine which admittedly uses some imported material. But I am confident that as the use of these machines increases Canadian manufacturers will produce models entirely made in Canada and when that is done we will be delighted to use them if the price is right. But we cannot use non-existent machines as the hon. member for St. Denis would have us do.
As far as the flying squads are concerned, the hon. member claimed that they were instituted by the present government as a camouflage for patronage or something of that nature. If he read the parliamentary return which was filed for him he would know that they were instituted long before this government came into power. He claims they are unfair to part-timers in the post office. This is just a complete lack of knowledge and appreciation of how the department operates. I can understand this. There is no conflict between the two groups. We have thousands of part-timers in the major cities of Canada and they work on a regular schedule. The flying squads are only on an intermittent basis. The hon. member says that flyings squads are being used for six to eight hours at a time. I very much doubt this. The matter comes under the direction of the local postmaster who is not supposed to do this. I am having an investigation made.
The hon. member referred to the transfer of post offices and suggested that there was something terrible in this. In the course of a year, Mr. Chairman, we switch from 1,000 to 1,500 post offices, with the average figure being somewhere around 1,200. This has been going on year in and year out for a long time. There are perfectly legitimate reasons for it such as retirement under the provisions of the Public Service Superannuation Act, dismissals where a man is removed from office for cause such as misappropriation of post office funds, unsatisfactory management, etc., resignations where the postmaster has requested to be relieved of the postmastership, and replacements where the postmaster is changed under the policy that all postmasters in revenue offices are to be replaced upon reaching the age of 70.
The hon. member for St. Denis said this was a terrible thing and that we were firing all these people for political reasons. I deny that categorically. I remind him of the fact that when the Liberal government came into power in 1935 they proceeded for partisan reasons to fire 350 postmasters. That is on the record. We have had to remove eight or nine-I do not remember the exact figure- for partisan reasons, each one following a full inquiry and complete support of the accusation made.

The hon. member made one of his big plays, of course, on the basis of thefts. Very briefly the basic story and background on this subject are contained in my first remarks and show that the situation has improved. At one point the hon. member quoted prosecution figures and complained about them having increased. Goodness gracious, what does he expect us to do, not prosecute people? I suppose if we did not prosecute them he certainly would have something to say. I think this is an indication that he was not clear as to what he was talking about because I certainly have no desire or intention of reducing prosecutions for thefts and burglaries.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I said it was a report from the Postmaster General himself and referred to all kinds of thefts, by people outside as well as people inside. If this report is accurate it is not the same report as the one he mentioned in the house today. If he wants me to repeat the figures I am ready to do so.

speakerposition: Postmaster General

speechtext: Is that the annual amount?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
Yes, $20 million annually. Taking these figures into consideration, the situation actually is that instead of a deficit of $173,000 in 1959 the two figures bring us to a deficit of $13,673,000. I ask him to remember that historically accommodation and banking has always been accounted for on the same basis so these figures are not new in any way. They are not comparable with the direct figures for previous years in the report of the Post Office Department.
He asked about the reduction in the number of post offices. This, of course, reflects the extension of our rural routes, the extension of letter carrier routes in the cities, the growing movement of people to the cities and
Supply-Post Office
the decline in the small communities. In many cases, these communities just disappear completely. We do not deliberately close small post offices, but we do find-I appreciate the hon. member's views-that in most large cities we have not yet reached the point of diminishing returns so far as post offices are concerned. On the other hand, in some places we have. In Toronto and Montreal, for instance, this is certainly the case with our metropolitan post offices. However, we are not doing this to build up bigger post offices in the cities; I can assure him of that.
The hon. member claimed that post office buildings were not being proceeded with quickly enough. I think that he overlooked, in that connection, the fact that while we do have 11,500 post offices, actually 8,000 of those are small revenue post offices where the postmaster has the responsibility of supplying the premises in a part of his store or something of that sort. Then there are another 1,750 sub-post offices located in stores in large cities, and the remainder are semistaff and staff offices. These are larger offices, but even in the case of some semi-staff offices, the premises are rented. When we say we built 65 post offices last year and 105 this year, I believe that is a very good record. It certainly shows we are going in the direction that the hon. member wants with 105 buildings this year.
I do not believe it would be practical to keep the wickets open 24 hours a day as the hon. member suggested. The short answer to this is that in the major centres we keep the wickets open in a pattern designed to match the business which offers. If we could get adequate business until ten o'clock at night in the main post office in Montreal, it would be kept open. If we find there are only one or two people between eleven and seven in the morning, then we will not keep it open.
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo spoke a little while ago, and I would tell him that the classification of post offices does not rest on revenue but rests on a unit of work basis. Then, in turn, the postmaster's salary is determined on the classification of the post office, not on the amount of revenue from that post office. He wants more government post office buildings in small communities. I can sympathize with him in that. Unfortunately we have to have a standard policy across Canada, and the one we have gives adequate weight to this particular consideration. I do agree with him that there has been inequities in so far as postmaster-telegraphers are concerned in Newfoundland. I do not agree with him that we have any responsibility for this, and I have made it quite clear to Canadian National Telegraphs that either

Supply-Post Office
they are going to do something about this or, alternatively, we just cannot go on being represented as their agents and taking responsibility for their actions. I think this is now fairly clearly understood. I must say I spent some time with the postmasters down there and I was very disappointed that they -not through any effort of the hon. member -seemed to have the idea that there was a measure of responsibility in the Post Office Department for this. I think they now understand the different situation.
Briefly, in closing, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway asked me about our attitude toward automation. I think perhaps I can sum it up this way. The issue on mechanization is the improved efficiency and handling of the mail, not the reduction of staff. The introduction of mechanical and electronic machinery will effect this in several ways: First, and most important, while it will not enable us immediately to reduce staff, it will enable us to handle more mail with the same staff. Second, its introduction will mean where we now use unskilled or semiskilled personnel in large numbers on a part-time basis, we will be able to introduce a lesser number of specially trained and fulltime postal employees. Finally, it will add substantially to our efficiency because in some of our larger cities, such as Toronto and Montreal, we are reaching a point where there are so many street names and divisions of streets to be remembered that the sortation process is slowed down by the inability of most of our staffs to memorize every division. Certainly there will be changes, and we know that this will mean a larger percentage of our total staff will be skilled, and more fulltime employees as opposed to part-time personnel.
Our full-time personnel are interested in this, and this is an encouraging thing. They are giving us, so far as I can see, support for it. We are not meeting any resistance. There are some who question this new development, although not the hon. member. There are some who feel there is an obligation on a government department, simply because it is a government department, to avoid improving its methods of operation so that by remaining inefficient an ever increasing number of jobs will be produced at the taxpayers' expense. This is not my view. If I may illustrate vividly how shortsighted and foolish such a policy would be, I would point out that within the memory of many people in the post office department letters from street letter boxes were picked up by men on foot carrying bags over their shoulders. I have no doubt that when the horse-drawn vehicles were introduced for this purpose

there were complaints that, in its search for efficiency, the post office department was threatening men with the loss of their jobs by departing from tradition. This is an attitude we do not have today.
I think that deals with most of the questions which were asked, and perhaps we might be able to proceed with the individual items.
Except mine.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
I have about ten seconds, perhaps I can get through with yours, too. The hon. member dealt, first, with the question of the remunera-ion of postal employees. He will understand, as a result of his long experience in the house, that he should really bring that to the attention of my colleague, the Minister of Finance. Then the hon. member dealt with money packages. The short answer to that is that in so far as adjoining cities are concerned, the banks are supposed to, and so far as I know do, transfer these by security transfer vehicles. In some cases, because of the distance between adjoining cities, 10 to 15 miles apart, they have been using the mails. We have had conversations with them, as the hon. member has said, urging them to eliminate this practice wherever possible. I take the view that money packages should go whenever possible by express or by security vehicle. On the other hand, I accept the fact that where there is no means of transportation except the post office, we have a responsibility to carry these packages. These are not the cases of which the hon. member was speaking.
Finally, so far as publishers' mail is concerned, the distribution of publications, I would merely say to him that this operation shows up as a loss on the operating statement of the Post Office Department. However, I take the view, and past governments have done, and I am sure succeeding governments will do, that we have a responsibility to enable the free and easy flow of information to all people in this country, and that magazines, books and newspapers, as well as other printed material of this sort, which helps to inform our people and raise the level of information, are entitled to consideration when postal rates are set.

I should like to continue this discussion when these estimates come up again. The minister cannot get away with that type of fast answer on this important subject.

Mr. Etheridge identified himself to him, and he admitted that he was Leslie Meehan, and he admitted that the picture in our possession was his, and we walked into the bedroom and a woman was lying in the bed, and when Mr. Etheridge asked her her name she sat in the bed; she was wearing blue and white pyjamas and she had her hair in pin curls; she gave her name as Violet Mitchell; and they both admitted living together as man and wife. Mr. Etheridge told both of them that they would hear from his real wife's attorneys in the near future, and we left the house.
It is unfortunate we cannot refer to other matters.
Are you getting tired of reading? Why not keep on reading?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
This is a simple case. The detectives got all the evidence they needed. Nothing was left to chance. The girl gave her name and they accepted it. I assume they felt they could serve her at that address because she was not asked for her address. Unless the wife has a wealthy boy friend then I presume the money for this divorce is coming from her parents with whom she went back to live. All the indications are that an agreement was reached between all the parties. I suggest they had a rehearsal and maybe the corespondent liked the respondent's company and moved in. It appears that her address will be the same as the respondent's. There has been no attempt to prove adultery. We are asked to dissolve the marriage on the grounds of adultery. We know what adultery is although many hon. members formerly were not aware. These detectives do not indicate that they yet understand what it is and Canadians generally are not aware of what we consider as adultery.
Point No. 6 of the petition reads as follows:
That your petitioner has ascertained that the respondent, Leslie Patrick Meehan did commit adultery on January 19, 1959, at 4196 Wellington street, Verdun, with Violet Mitchell, who resides at 4196 Wellington street, Verdun.
I hazard a guess that he did commit adultery with her but no one could ascertain that from reading the evidence before us. It is only a supposition on my part that adultery took place. If we were well read we could probably tell you what book she was reading when the detectives visited.
Parliament could grant this divorce and hon. members feel that they had done a good job. No children are involved. The parties are young and at least one could go on to make a good marriage. I do not think we


should insist, therefore, on a closer examination of this obviously flimsy, fabricated evidence.

Before we proceed further, I wonder whether I might make a few comments about this. But first, because of the reference of my hon. friend from Timiskam-ing, may I say that it is not my intention to engage in any discussion about the excellent, enlightening and revealing telecast which took place last night.
There are a few matters with which my hon. friend from Timiskaming dealt. He indicated that the evidence was presented generally in a clear-cut way but there are a few things on which I think perhaps I should comment. The hon. member for Victoria, (B.C.), who is an esteemed member of the legal profession and who is now substituting for the hon. member for Halifax who is engaged on other matters in the province of Nova Scotia, I understand, will perhaps clear up this point when I make reference to it.
One of the first things that came to my mind-I only do this because of our reading and examination of evidence in other cases and thus compare this with the others-is the following which appears on page 11 where the first question directed to Mr. Etheridge is answered in this way. First, he identifies the picture as being that of the respondent; he gives the name of the respondent and then he says:
And a picture you gave to us when you retained our services in the fall of 1958.
Other evidence given by the petitioner was to the effect that the wife stopped living with her husband in December of 1958. I know that in quite a number of other cases, Mr. Chairman, whoever is counsel for the petitioner inquires of the petitioner when she or he came to see him, when those services were retained. In other cases, the time is given, the particular month of the particular year when she or he first went to see the lawyer about whatever difficulties he or she had with the spouse. In this one we find that while the petitioner ceased living with the husband as husband and wife in December, 1958, as shown by the petitioner's evidence, in fact the petitioner had undoubtedly-if we give full credit to Mr. Etheridge's testimony-retained the services of Mr. Jacobs, or went to see Mr. Jacobs, sometime before they actually stopped living together, because he retained the services of Messrs. Etheridge and Brault of the Reliable Detective Agency, bureau, or whatever it is, in the fall of 1958.
I do not say there is any conflict there. I do not say that this is a point that is earthshaking or is going to influence us or upset

us in the consideration which the committee should give to this particular case; but I would have thought that it would be well for this point to be cleared up and some specific reference made to when the young lady went first to see the lawyer. As I say, I do not think it has any bearing on the case. Perhaps it is one of the things on which, for use and for understanding in the particular case before us and for use and our guidance in the future, the hon. member for Victoria, (B.C.) might be able, from his legal experience, to give us an indication of just how it happens in this particular case that there seems to be a little conflict in the time.
I also wish to reiterate, if I may do so without transgressing on the rules by the use of repetition and, to make reference to, as the hon. member for Timiskaming has done, the fortuitous circumstances which existed and which led the detectives at eleven o'clock, or eleven thirty o'clock in the evening just to walk into somebody's apartment. I say, as I have said on many other occasions, Mr. Chairman, this just does not happen with the degree of regularity that we are asked to believe it happens. It may happen in an isolated instance. It may be that in this instance the respondent is in the habit of opening his doors at eleven o'clock in the evening after all the lights are out, after he has been in bed, to people who-it was two people, incidentally in this case-are complete strangers.

The hon. member must restrict his remarks to the bill and those discursive remarks as to what may be done in certain circumstances, while they may be interesting, have no relation to the bill. His remarks must be related to the bill.

May I make a comment on the point of order and say I do not think it is a point of order because my remarks were related to this bill, were related to the evidence given by Mr. Etheridge. I just happened to read the evidence. If my hon. friend from Victoria, (B.C.) wants me to read the evidence I can do so. The evidence given by Mr. Etheridge is that he and his partner at eleven o'clock in the evening went up and knocked on the door; the door was opened and they were given free access to the apartment. I say it is highly unlikely that this did take place.
On a point of order, if my hon. friend wishes to read the evidence-

I am not sure which point of order I am discussing now; I think it is the first one. I was saying that my remarks were completely in order and completely relevant to the particular bill before us because the bill asks us to dissolve the marriage on the ground of adultery. It is mentioned in the bill itself and I am talking about that particular evidence and the manner in which the evidence of adultery was obtained. I am casting doubts on whether we should accept that or not.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) is going to raise another point of order?

Mr. Chairman, all I want to say is that the hon. member is entitled to comment on the evidence, but he is not entitled to comment upon generalities of the giving of evidence in these cases, as he has been doing.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member for Skeena realizes that he cannot discuss procedure. That is the point the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) is making.

That is not my intention or desire, Mr. Chairman. I am just pointing out -if I can repeat this to get it clear on the record and clear in the mind of the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.)-that this adultery was alleged to have taken place on the third floor of a three-flat building. To quote from the evidence of Mr. Etheridge, about half-way through, he says this:
At 10.35 we noted that the third floor was in complete darkness. At eleven o'clock-
Twenty five minutes later, allowing for what they thought was necessary time in their experience to elapse, he continues:
At eleven o'clock we went to the inside stairs and groped our way to the third landing.
They groped their way up three flights of stairs. I imagine this must have been in complete darkness, or perhaps the two detectives were not able to see too well on this particular evening. In any event, for one reason or another, they had to grope their way to the third landing. Once they got there they knocked on the door and the respondent came to the door and asked who it was. They told him they were from the Reliable Detective Bureau; they wanted to speak to him, and these were the open sesame words that allowed these two gentlemen, complete strangers to the respondent, to walk into the apartment and ask all manner of questions which have been gone into quite extensively by the hon. member for Timiskaming. I submit, Mr. Chairman, and

Private Bills-Divorce
I think I am perfectly in order in doing so, that this sort of thing just does not occur. At the risk of offending the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) again, may I reiterate that the respondent in this instance may have developed a habit of opening his door to all and sundry at eleven o'clock in the evening-
Maybe he opened the door to let the cat out and they walked in.

He let a couple of somethings in. I would not call them by the designation the hon. member has used. In any event, unless 'he is in the habit of doing this sort of thing in the case of anybody who happens to come along at eleven o'clock in the evening, it is stretching the point quite a bit to ask us to believe that it occurred in this way, especially after groping up three flights of stairs in darkness to get there.
There is another matter to which I wish to make reference. It has to do with the evidence of Mr. Etheridge and Mr. Brault and the so-called admission that the respondent and the corespondent were living there as man and wife and that they both admitted this was so. I should like to quote part of the evidence of Mr. Etheridge starting at the bottom of page 11 and going over to page 12 in which he relates the story of his conversation with the respondent. He talked about an admission and said:
He admitted that he was not living with his real wife-
He gives her name.
-but admitted that he was living with another woman.
I do not know if this question was asked by Mr. Jacobs or Senator Roebuck but I would take it to be Senator Roebuck.
Q. Tell us about that admission. What was said that led to such statements?
A. I said to him, "We know you are living here with another woman as man and wife, not your real wife-
He gives her name.
-and he admitted to that.
So we have secondhand information that the respondent admitted that he was living there as man and wife with someone who was not his legally married wife. He goes on from there to describe the setting of the bedroom and the apparel of the corespondent.

On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, I can only say that the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) seems to have the ability today to raise all sorts of inaccurate things which are not in fact points of order. This question has been dealt with on a number of occasions. In fact, we have had points of order raised by my hon. friend's colleagues that we should not be reading the evidence and your ruling was that we could read it, discuss it and make reference to it in any way whatsoever with the qualification that we must deal with that part of the evidence relating strictly to the material in the bill before us. That is what I am attempting to do. I am not trying to put any better words on the record. I am merely following the rules of the house about repetition. If I were to read from the evidence the description of the bedroom, what he or she was wearing and so on I would be repeating what the hon. member for Timiskaming read when he was discussing this case. I want to stay within the rules. All the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) is doing is inviting me to violate the rules, and I do not think I can accept his invitation.
Then there was another question, "How was she dressed?" and the first statement is that she was wearing certain things. Here is the next one and it is this statement I want to take issue with.
Why don't you read it? Why don't you give the answer?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. Will the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) please resume his seat? Will the hon. member please sit down? When the hon. member wishes to rise he must address the Chair. The hon. member for Skeena has the floor.
I do not want to cause-

Skeena has the floor but I am rising on a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I will be very happy to hear the point of order.

We usually find that these members say they have the floor when we raise any point, but I wish to say this. The hon. member for Skeena read a question and then he proceeded to give his own extemporaneous version of the answer. I contend that is completely out of order. If he reads a question from the record then he must read the answer and not give us his interpretation of the answer.

speechtext: Order. The hon. member-
May I speak to the point of order?
