speechtext: Certainly.

I do not know what the difficulty is with the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) today but apparently it is something that should not find expression in this house. I read the question that was asked. The question was, "How was she dressed?" The first part of the answer as to what she was wearing is not relevant to the point I wish to make. I was about to read the second part which is relevant to the point I wish to make and unfortunately the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.), with his blood pressure and other problems jumped to some conclusion just to get on the record and caused some confusion.
That is not my problem. I know what yours are.
I submit that is not a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: With respect to the question of whether or not the hon. member should read the question in the evidence and then the exact words of the answer, the hon. member can give his own interpretation of the answer as long as he does not change the meaning. The Chair sees nothing wrong with that.
You have been wrong four times, today, Bert.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.

Here is the answer to which I wish to refer, and to avoid any exercise being necessary on the part of the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) I will read it.
They both had admitted that they were living together as man and wife at the premises-
Then the address is given. I hope the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) will not raise a point of order about that because it is not my practice to read the actual address or the names of the individuals in order to prevent any undue publicity. The witness said:
They both had admitted that they were living together as man and wife-
Up to this time, Mr. Chairman, they both had not admitted they were living there as man and wife. The only person who admitted they were living as man and wife was the respondent. It was given in previous evidence that he had so admitted. The only evidence before or after that as to what the corespondent said is that she gave her name, and it is put in quotation marks. That is the only evidence here as to what she said. I submit that the evidence does not show that she admitted they were living as man and
Private Bills-Divorce
wife. Only one person admitted it and that was the respondent himself. The witness went on to say:
We were at the doorway of the bedroom and they both could hear us talking when the admissions were made.
I assume he is talking about the admissions by the respondent that they were living there as man and wife. He is undoubtedly jumping to the conclusion that the corespondent agreed with this admission by silence, but nowhere in the evidence does it appear that she admitted that they were living there as man and wife. Mr. Brault said exactly the same thing in his evidence on page 13. He said:
and they both admitted living together as man and wife.
I submit this is not true. Mr. Etheridge and Mr. Brault either did not give the full evidence in the first place as to what was admitted or they are not giving the correct evidence. Now they say both people admitted it, and there is a conflict between them. Unfortunately that has been the pattern with these gentlemen. They have been too carefree in the manner in which they have given evidence before the committee of the other place, knowing full well that as long as their sketchy evidence meets the basic test that is all that is necessary. If there is any laxity or incorrect evidence this is a minor detail.
I think there is another thing which should have been cleared up in conection with this case. Again I would indicate to you, sir, and through you to the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.), that in my following remarks I wish to make a brief reference to the way in which I think evidence should be given, and relate it to evidence which we have heard in other cases. I only do this in an incidental way for the sake of comparison, and I think I will be in order in so doing. This is alleged to be a so-called common law relationship, that is a man and a woman not legally married but living together as man and wife.
In other cases-this is where I may run foul of the rules, but I do not think I will- the test to be met in determining whether or not a common law arrangement is proven is how long they have lived together. How long has this relationship existed? In some instances we have found the relationship existed for two, three or more years, at least for long periods of time. In one case with which we dealt a few days ago the period was only two months, and you will recall that I wondered whether or not that was a sufficient period of time in which to establish a common law relationship.
In this instance, so far as we know from the evidence, the common law relationship

Private Bills-Divorce
existed for one evening, that is January 19, 1959. The evidence indicates that the respondent had seen the corespondent and had been seen in her company on occasions, and had been seen going in and out of this particular address where the adultery is alleged to have occurred on the 19th. However, so far as living together as man and wife is concerned, this relationship existed for one day, January 19, 1959. If that is the type of evidence that the investigators are going to give to the committee of the other place and are going to ask us in this house to accept as part of the corroborating evidence of the common law relationship, then they should also be prepared to go into the question of how long that man and wife relationship has existed. Otherwise, I do not think such evidence should be in there. We know that in giving weight to evidence submitted, in this instance to the committee of the other place, and certainly so far as the courts themselves are concerned, if proof can be given that there is a common law relationship then the court and the committee of the other place will give a great deal of weight to that as, in fact, proving the alleged adultery.
When we talk here about people living together as man and wife, the same design is there. It is an attempt to prove, through the common law relationship, that adultery could have or was likely to have taken place. If these gentlemen, Mr. Etheridge and Mr. Brault or the lawyer who is handling this case, expect us to give weight or that degree of weight which is necessary to the evidence concerning a common law relationship, then they should be duty-bound to put in evidence concerning the period of time during which that common law relationship has existed. In my opinion, regardless of what these gentlemen say about the time during which the common law relationship existed, they lived together as man and wife for one evening only, which would put this case in the same category as the motel and hotel cases.
That is sufficient, is it not?

My friend's voice is getting out of whack. That may be sufficient if they are not going to talk about the common law relationship. In any case, where the motel or hotel type of evidence is used, it is obviously arranged in a large number of cases, regardless of Mr. Robinette of the law society of Upper Canada saying that he has no knowledge of this sort of thing. I think he is talking through his hat. There is knowledge that a great deal of collusion exists in these one-night stands or hotel and motel cases.

This is substantially what exists here, and we must look at it in that light, especially when there is no reference as to the time they have been living together as man and wife.
1	raise this point, not to object to the granting of the divorce, but to point out to hose lawyers who are making a living off these unfortunate cases, and to the investigators who are making their living off these cases, that they had better be a bit more careful in the future in their presentation of the evidence. If parliament is going to have to deal with these cases in the future, and I hope we do not, I think we should raise this point. As I say, I do not raise it to object to the case, I merely raise it because, as my friend from Timiskaming said, the evidence was presented in a sloppy fashion without too much regard for the fact that there was conflict between the evidence given by the two investigators. If they wish to have the evidence that they give considered in the future then they should smarten up and attempt to present their points in a proper fashion without these conflicts.
